issues.description: The study reconstructs past episodes using retrospective self-report, but the manuscript describes this as a "prospective" design. That is conceptually incorrect and overstates the strength of temporal inference. Retrospective recall cannot establish prospective prediction or real-time identification of imminent risk.
issues.quote: By reconstructing the timeline of recent suicidal behaviors through a retrospective clinical interview, we utilized a prospective research design to understand which features in text communications predicted suicide attempt

issues.description: The manuscript repeatedly claims the work informs real-time assessment, but all episodes were identified retrospectively and no model was prospectively evaluated in real time. This overstates what the data can support and risks misleading readers about clinical readiness.
issues.quote: To this end, we aimed to improve our ability to assess suicide risk dynamically in real time.

issues.description: Slope comparisons are not validly matched across conditions. Attempt episodes are anchored to a concrete event (the attempt), whereas ideation, depressed/high-stress, and typical/positive episodes are arbitrary two-week windows without an equivalent anchor event. Comparing trajectories toward a real event versus trajectories within arbitrary windows can create artifactual differences.
issues.quote: Episodes included: 1) past actual, interrupted, or aborted suicide attempts, using the one-week period prior to the attempt as a “suicide attempt episode”; 2) two-week episodes of suicide ideation (not resulting in a suicide attempt); 3) two-week episodes of depressed mood or high stress (not resulting in suicide ideation or attempt); and 4) two-week episode of typical mood

issues.description: The manuscript inconsistently defines the focal pre-attempt window as both one week and two weeks. This directly affects reproducibility and interpretation of the temporal analyses.
issues.quote: Mixed-effects models tested whether these constructs differed in general (means) and over time (slopes) two weeks before a suicide attempt, relative to lower-risk periods. / Episodes included: 1) past actual, interrupted, or aborted suicide attempts, using the one-week period prior to the attempt as a “suicide attempt episode”

issues.description: The primary "attempt" condition includes actual attempts, interrupted attempts, aborted attempts, and even episodes with no enacted self-harm. This broadens the outcome far beyond standard suicide attempt definitions and mixes clinically distinct states, threatening validity of conclusions about "suicide attempts."
issues.quote: (Note that reported ‘suicide attempts’ also included incidents in which no physical attempt was enacted but in which participants considered their planning or actions to constitute a higher level of suicidal intent than ‘suicide ideation’ so they subjectively endorsed making an attempt on the screener questions.)

issues.description: Most analyzed "attempt" episodes did not involve physical harm, yet the paper draws conclusions about markers preceding suicide attempts. This substantially weakens construct validity and may explain why findings may not generalize to medically serious or enacted attempts.
issues.quote: Based on participants’ description of the objective lethality of the attempt, 29% of incidents involved some action being taken in which some physical harm was caused ... while 71% of incidents did not result in any physical harm

issues.description: Participants with substantial current suicidal desire, plan, or intent were excluded. This creates spectrum restriction and limits relevance to the very population for whom imminent-risk tools are most needed.
issues.quote: Inclusion criteria included ... (4) minimal or no current desire to die ... Any participants with intense thoughts of suicide who were determined to be at “high risk” or “imminent risk” for suicidal behavior ... were excluded from study participation

issues.description: Eligibility depended on having retrievable historical messaging data. This likely selected for participants with particular phone habits, device continuity, backup practices, and recency of episodes, which can bias both the sample and which episodes were analyzable.
issues.quote: Inclusion criteria included ... availability of and access to personal messaging data dating back prior to significant life events (e.g., suicide attempt)

issues.description: Historical text data were incompletely recoverable, especially from iPhones and older devices. This means the analyzed dataset is a selective subset of all messages and likely favors more recent episodes; the missingness is unlikely to be random.
issues.quote: Though most text data was successfully extracted from both Android and iPhone devices, a number of iPhone users had encryption settings on their phones that prevented third-party iPhone software from accessing text data. ... efforts to collection additional messages outside of their current mobile device were minimally successful.

issues.description: Less than half of queried episodes had SMS data, and only 27 of 33 participants contributed analyzable episodes. Mixed models do not solve bias from missing-not-at-random data, especially when missingness depends on device history, backup behavior, and episode recency.
issues.quote: Among the episodes queried during the lab interview, 134 (46%) episodes contained SMS data, collected from 27 different participants.

issues.description: The sample is small and demographically narrow: mostly female, White, college-aged, and largely some-college students. Findings are unlikely to generalize to older adults, men, more diverse populations, or clinical populations with different texting habits.
issues.quote: Most of the participants were female, White, and college-aged.

issues.description: Recruitment began with a participant-pool prescreen requiring endorsement of past sadness/hopelessness and willingness to be contacted. This introduces strong self-selection and may miss individuals with different symptom profiles or lower willingness to disclose suicidal history.
issues.quote: On the participant pool pretest ... participants were asked, “Have you ever had a period of sadness in the past during which you felt hopeless?” and, if so, they were then asked whether they would like to be contacted about possible participation in studies that ask more questions about this period of time in their life.

issues.description: The manuscript does not state that LIWC analyses were limited to participant-authored outgoing texts. "Each individual SMS message" implies received messages may also have been analyzed, meaning key language features could reflect the language of other people rather than the participant. That is a major construct-validity problem for claims about the participant’s self-focus or affect.
issues.quote: Each individual SMS message was inputted into and scored using the 2015 version of Linguistic Inquiry and Word Count (LIWC)

issues.subcategory: LIWC applied to single short messages
issues.description: Scoring individual SMS messages with LIWC is problematic because texts are often extremely short, sparse, abbreviated, and context-dependent. LIWC category proportions on very short texts are unstable and can be dominated by one or two words, increasing noise and false positives.
issues.quote: Each individual SMS message was inputted into and scored using the 2015 version of Linguistic Inquiry and Word Count (LIWC)

issues.description: The study treats first-person singular pronouns as rumination/self-focus and sent/received message ratios as belongingness or burdensomeness. These are very indirect proxies for complex constructs, and the manuscript provides no validation that these SMS-derived metrics measure those constructs in this context.
issues.quote: we tested whether use of first-person pronouns (as an indicator of rumination) was greater prior to suicide attempts ... by examining patterns in outgoing vs. incoming messages.

issues.description: Comparison episodes are heterogeneous and inconsistently defined: ideation, depressed mood or high stress, and typical mood, elsewhere referred to as positive mood. Mixing depressed mood with high stress and typical mood with positive mood makes comparator conditions poorly defined and difficult to interpret.
issues.quote: 3) two-week episodes of depressed mood or high stress (not resulting in suicide ideation or attempt); and 4) two-week episode of typical mood (i.e., neither particularly positive nor negative mood and no ideation or attempt).

issues.subcategory: subjective episode classification without standardized rules
issues.description: The entire within-subject design depends on participant-selected episode dates and labels, but the manuscript does not provide standardized operational rules, adjudication procedures, or interrater reliability for episode classification. Asking follow-up questions is not equivalent to a reproducible classification protocol.
issues.quote: During the interview, participants were asked to identify a number of specific events or episodes in the past and the calendar dates during which the episodes took place. ... Participants answered additional questions about each reported episode as a way to minimize the risk of misclassification

issues.subcategory: unclear selection when more than three episodes existed
issues.description: The study capped collection at three episodes per type, but does not explain how episodes were chosen when participants had more than three. Choosing recent, memorable, or severe episodes could introduce selection bias and analytic flexibility.
issues.quote: For each episode type, we asked about a maximum of three episodes (e.g., three suicide attempts if participant has three or more lifetime attempts).

issues.description: The time window was not cleanly prespecified. The manuscript says episodes were set to two weeks, but then says the optimal window was assessed empirically using visual inspection of the same dataset. This is analytic flexibility that can inflate apparent effects.
issues.quote: The decision to set each episode at two weeks long was made in a conservative effort ... The question of the optimal time window was also assessed empirically, using visual inspection of descriptive figures to identify when the rate of change appeared to be most pronounced.

issues.description: The time variable includes day 0, but day 0 is the day of the attempt. Unless messages after the attempt were excluded, the analysis may mix pre-attempt communication with communication during or after the suicidal act, hospitalization, or social response to the crisis.
issues.quote: day of episode (numerical factor ranging from -14 to 0)

issues.description: The manuscript describes day of episode as a "numerical factor," which is contradictory. It is unclear whether time was modeled as continuous linear, categorical, or numerically coded factor. This ambiguity impairs reproducibility and interpretation of the reported "slopes."
issues.quote: day of episode (numerical factor ranging from -14 to 0)

issues.subcategory: inappropriate model family for counts and ratios
issues.description: The manuscript states that non-proportion outcomes such as number of messages per day were analyzed with linear mixed models using the raw values. Message counts are count data and sent/received ratios are bounded/skewed and can be undefined; treating them as Gaussian continuous variables is generally inappropriate and can distort inference.
issues.quote: For outcome variables that were not proportion scores (e.g., number of messages sent per day), the raw continuous variable was used in a linear mixed-effects model (LMM)

issues.description: Converting LIWC percentages to counts and modeling category-word versus non-category-word proportions treats words within a message as binomial trials. Words within a text are not independent Bernoulli trials, and sparse/short texts likely induce overdispersion and zero inflation. No diagnostics or correction are reported.
issues.quote: These LIWC percentage scores were converted into counts and then entered as proportions in our models (i.e., number of words in a given text message belonging to versus not belonging to the LIWC category)

issues.description: Including a random intercept for "message" is unusual because each message is typically a single observation. For Gaussian models this is redundant with residual error; for GLMMs it acts like an observation-level random effect but no rationale is given. The random-effects structure is not clearly justified and is difficult to reproduce.
issues.quote: a maximal random effects model, which included random intercepts of participant, episode, and message, and random by-participant slopes, was used

issues.subcategory: convergence failure and simplified random effects
issues.description: The main interaction analyses did not support the planned random-effects structure; all random slopes were dropped because models did not converge. This can materially change standard errors and inflate Type I error, especially for within-subject longitudinal effects.
issues.quote: Models with the full set of random slopes did not converge; therefore, no random slopes were included in the final model.

issues.description: Messages and days within an episode are serially correlated, but the model description includes no autocorrelation structure or other time-series handling. Ignoring temporal dependence can underestimate uncertainty and overstate significance of slope differences.
issues.quote: This approach also allowed us to maximize sources of variance by analyzing on the message level rather than only mean values by episode

issues.description: The study runs many omnibus tests and pairwise contrasts across numerous LIWC variables and two analysis families, yet explicitly declines any multiplicity control. Given the small sample and many p-values hovering near .05, the false-positive risk is substantial.
issues.quote: Given this is a pilot study with a small and already potentially underpowered sample and the fact that we did not have concrete directional hypotheses for many of the tests, we decided not to artificially suppress Type I error (i.e., using a multiple comparisons correction)

issues.subcategory: power analysis not appropriate for the actual models
issues.description: The power analysis is not convincing for the reported mixed-effects analyses. It uses Cramer’s V for chi-square tests, assumes large effects from unrelated between-subject studies, and contains opaque arithmetic about "60 attempts but only 20 with collected, usable SMS data, divided by the design effect." This does not transparently justify power for the fitted multilevel models.
issues.quote: We determined that a sample size of 30 suicide attempters (representing 60 attempts but only 20 with collected, usable SMS data, divided by the design effect) would provide enough power to detect only large effect sizes (Cramer’s V=0.29) for chi-square tests of mixed-effects models

issues.description: The discussion claims mean differences showed greater anxiety before attempts, but the results section states anxiety was not significant. This is a substantive misreporting of the findings.
issues.quote: In terms of overall mean differences, few reliable differences emerged though results indicated that the period of high risk just before a suicide attempt was associated with messages indicating greater anxiety and sadness. / No significant effects by episode type emerged for more general emotional content ... or other specific emotions/constructs (i.e., anxiety, anger, death).

issues.description: The same sadness omnibus test is reported with two different p-values in the paper (.003 in text, .033 in Table 2). This raises concern about reporting accuracy and which result is correct.
issues.quote: Regarding sentiment, there was a significant effect of episode type on use of sad words, 2(3)=8.74, p=.003. / Sadness (sad) | 2=8.74 | 3 | 3 | .033

issues.description: Episodes could come from very different points in participants’ lives, but the analyses do not account for calendar time, participant age at episode, or broad secular changes in texting behavior, relationships, or treatment. Within-person comparisons across years are therefore vulnerable to major confounding.
issues.quote: participants were asked to identify a number of specific events or episodes in the past ... Inclusion criteria included ... access to personal messaging data dating back prior to significant life events

issues.subcategory: within-subject claim weakened by sparse episode coverage
issues.description: The paper emphasizes a within-subject design, but participants contributed widely varying numbers of episode types and many had no usable data for some conditions. This means some contrasts are based on a sparse and uneven subset rather than robust within-person comparisons across all four states.
issues.quote: participants varied widely in terms of the number of episodes types they reported and for which they had text data. ... Among the episodes queried during the lab interview, 134 (46%) episodes contained SMS data, collected from 27 different participants.

issues.description: The manuscript conflates likelihood-ratio tests and Wald chi-square tests, which are not the same procedure. This makes the inferential method unclear.
issues.quote: Likelihood-ratio (Wald chi-square) tests were performed to compare goodness of fit for models including and excluding the fixed effect of episode type.

issues.description: Messages were pooled across all recipients, but language varies dramatically by interlocutor (partner, parent, friend, automated service). Not modeling recipient/contact can confound apparent risk markers with shifts in who the participant was texting.
issues.quote: all available SMS data from each device were downloaded (i.e., not from only certain dates or recipients).

issues.description: The study relied on multiple third-party extraction tools across platforms, but does not report any validation that extracted message histories were complete, correctly timestamped, or deduplicated. Differential extraction error across devices could bias episode comparisons.
issues.quote: SMS text message data from iPhone and Android phones were accessed using third-party software or phone applications.

issues.description: A significant result is reported for LIWC "Tone," but the manuscript itself acknowledges that some LIWC variables are proprietary and non-transparent. Using opaque variables limits interpretability and reproducibility, especially when such variables contribute to substantive conclusions.
issues.quote: Other LIWC variables include counts of words ... and several proprietary, “non-transparent” variables (e.g., Tone)
